The user is describing a bug where the radio player shows as "playing" but the actual audio stream has been disconnected (e.g., after switching tabs, closing the app, or the device going to sleep). I need to explore how the radio player works to understand the current state management and audio handling, then propose a fix.

Let me explore the relevant files.

I've read through the full `useRadioPlayer.ts` implementation. The root cause is clear: there are no `visibilitychange` or audio health checks, so when the browser silently kills the stream in the background (especially on iOS PWA / mobile), the React state stays `isPlaying: true` while `audio.paused` is actually `true`.

Now I understand the issue. The problem is:

1. When the user switches tabs/windows or closes the app, the browser may suspend or disconnect the audio stream
2. The `isPlaying` state can remain `true` even though the audio has actually stopped
3. The `HTMLAudioElement` fires a `pause` event when the browser suspends audio, but there might be cases where it doesn't

The key issue is that for live radio streams, the browser can silently stop playback without firing appropriate events, especially on mobile (iOS PWA). The `pause` event handler does exist but it checks `reconnectingRef.current` which could mask the issue.


I need to add visibility detection to catch when the page comes back into focus and verify the audio state is still accurate, plus listen for additional audio events like stalled or suspend that might indicate playback issues. The most reliable fix is checking the actual audio element's paused state against our React state whenever the page becomes visible again. The `pause` event handler should catch disconnections, but browsers handle stream failures inconsistently—some don't fire the pause event, others leave the audio element in an ambiguous state, especially on iOS. I'll add a `visibilitychange` listener to reconcile the actual audio state when the app regains focus, and potentially a periodic heartbeat check while playing to catch silent stream failures.

    14|# Fix Stale Playback State on Stream Disconnect
    15|
    16|## Problem
    17|
    18|When the user switches away from the app or the device goes to sleep, the browser (especially iOS Safari in PWA mode) can silently disconnect the live radio stream. The `HTMLAudioElement` may not fire a `pause` or `error` event in all cases, leaving `isPlaying: true` in React state while the audio is actually stopped.
    19|
    20|## Root Cause
    21|
    22|[app/hooks/useRadioPlayer.ts](app/hooks/useRadioPlayer.ts) only listens for `playing`, `waiting`, `error`, and `pause` events on the audio element. There is no reconciliation when the page regains visibility, and no periodic check that the audio element's actual state matches the React state.
    23|
    24|## Fix: Two-Layer Detection
    25|
    26|Both layers go inside the existing `useEffect` block (lines 54-103) in `useRadioPlayer.ts`.
    27|
    28|### 1. Reconcile state on `visibilitychange`
    29|
    30|When the document becomes visible again, compare `isPlayingRef.current` against `audio.paused`. If React thinks we're playing but the audio element is actually paused (and we're not mid-reconnect), mark the player as paused:
    31|
    32|```typescript
    33|const onVisibilityChange = () => {
    34|  if (document.hidden) return;
    35|  if (!isPlayingRef.current) return;
    36|  if (reconnectingRef.current) return;
    37|
    38|  if (audio.paused) {
    39|    setIsPaused(true);
    40|    setIsPlaying(false);
    41|    setIsBuffering(false);
    42|    setMediaSessionPlaybackState("paused");
    43|  }
    44|};
    45|document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", onVisibilityChange);
    46|```
    47|
    48|Clean up in the same `useEffect` return block.
    49|
    50|### 2. Listen to `stalled` event
    51|
    52|The `stalled` event fires when the browser is trying to fetch media data but it is not forthcoming. For a live stream that silently dies, this is a strong signal. If we're supposed to be playing but the audio is stalled and paused, reconcile:
    53|
    54|```typescript
    55|const onStalled = () => {
    56|  if (reconnectingRef.current) return;
    57|  if (!isPlayingRef.current) return;
    58|  if (audio.paused) {
    59|    setIsPaused(true);
    60|    setIsPlaying(false);
    61|    setIsBuffering(false);
    62|    setMediaSessionPlaybackState("paused");
    63|  }
    64|};
    65|audio.addEventListener("stalled", onStalled);
    66|```
    67|

     1|# Fix Stale Playback State on Stream Disconnect
     2|
     3|## Problem
     4|
     5|When the user switches away from the app or the device goes to sleep, the browser (especially iOS Safari in PWA mode) can silently disconnect the live radio stream. The `HTMLAudioElement` may not fire a `pause` or `error` event in all cases, leaving `isPlaying: true` in React state while the audio is actually stopped.
     6|
     7|## Root Cause
     8|
     9|[app/hooks/useRadioPlayer.ts](app/hooks/useRadioPlayer.ts) only listens for `playing`, `waiting`, `error`, and `pause` events on the audio element. There is no reconciliation when the page regains visibility, and no periodic check that the audio element's actual state matches the React state.
    10|
    11|## Fix: Two-Layer Detection
    12|
    13|Both layers go inside the existing `useEffect` block (lines 54-103) in `useRadioPlayer.ts`.
    14|
    15|### 1. Reconcile state on `visibilitychange`
    16|
    17|When the document becomes visible again, compare `isPlayingRef.current` against `audio.paused`. If React thinks we're playing but the audio element is actually paused (and we're not mid-reconnect), mark the player as paused:
    18|
    19|```typescript
    20|const onVisibilityChange = () => {
    21|  if (document.hidden) return;
    22|  if (!isPlayingRef.current) return;
    23|  if (reconnectingRef.current) return;
    24|
    25|  if (audio.paused) {
    26|    setIsPaused(true);
    27|    setIsPlaying(false);
    28|    setIsBuffering(false);
    29|    setMediaSessionPlaybackState("paused");
    30|  }
    31|};
    32|document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", onVisibilityChange);
    33|```
    34|
    35|Clean up in the same `useEffect` return block.
    36|
    37|### 2. Listen to `stalled` event
    38|
    39|The `stalled` event fires when the browser is trying to fetch media data but it is not forthcoming. For a live stream that silently dies, this is a strong signal. If we're supposed to be playing but the audio is stalled and paused, reconcile:
    40|
    41|```typescript
    42|const onStalled = () => {
    43|  if (reconnectingRef.current) return;
    44|  if (!isPlayingRef.current) return;
    45|  if (audio.paused) {
    46|    setIsPaused(true);
    47|    setIsPlaying(false);
    48|    setIsBuffering(false);
    49|    setMediaSessionPlaybackState("paused");
    50|  }
    51|};
    52|audio.addEventListener("stalled", onStalled);
    53|```
    54|
    55|### Summary of changes
    56|
    57|All changes are in a single file: [app/hooks/useRadioPlayer.ts](app/hooks/useRadioPlayer.ts), inside the existing `useEffect` at line 54:
    58|
    59|- Add `onVisibilityChange` handler on `document`
    60|- Add `onStalled` handler on `audio`
    61|- Add corresponding cleanup in the return block
    62|
